Note (ha!) on 50A: Curved lines are used in musical scores for two purposes--to indicate slurs, and ties (joining two notes of the same pitch into one, with the sum of their durations). Has TIE, clued thus, ever appeared as an entry? Now, as one who has dabbled a bit in music typography and scorewriting (all done on computers, nowadays), there are many odd, often illogical, conventions and subtle distinctions made in music notation. For instance, the white note heads of whole notes vary slightly from those of half notes. (Sorry, non-musicians, this is a little inside baseball.) Are the curved lines used for slurs different than the ones used for ties? Slightly different thickness, perhaps? No, they're graphically identical. Now, one might argue that slurs always go over notes of different pitches, whereas ties go between notes of the same pitch, but there are still situations where you'd draw a slur over notes of the same pitch (usually in conjunction with other marks--staccato or tenuto marks, etc.) to notate certain types of string bowing effects, for instance. In Sean's example, “Ann gives the basketball to her teammate,” "teammate" is not an indirect object; it is the object of the preposition "to". “Ann gives her teammate the basketball” has "teammate" as the indirect object and is a much better analogy for the Latin dative. But in Latin, prepositions normally take the accusative or ablative case; a recipient such as this is expressed with the dative without a preposition.
